note: Quick Summaries (Topic + Summary), English; reviewed for the SiraatOne website.
s: The opening prayer: praising Allah, worshipping Him alone, and asking Him for guidance.

Al-Fatihah is the first surah of the Quran and, according to the great majority of scholars, was revealed in Makkah. It is a prayer the servant says to Allah. It begins by praising Him as Lord of all the worlds, the Most Merciful, and Master of the Day of Judgment. The servant then promises to worship Allah alone and to seek help from Him alone. Finally he asks Allah to guide him to the straight path of those He has blessed, away from the way of those who earned His anger and those who went astray. It is recited in every prayer. The Prophet ﷺ called it the greatest surah of the Quran and "the seven oft-repeated ayahs" (Sahih al-Bukhari).
Building the Muslim community on faith in Allah and obedience to His laws.

Al-Baqarah is the longest surah of the Quran and was among the first revealed in Madinah, while the Prophet ﷺ was building the Muslim community there. It begins by describing three kinds of people (the believers, the disbelievers and the hypocrites) and calls all mankind to worship Allah alone. It tells the story of Adam and reminds the Children of Israel of Allah's favors and the covenants they broke. This includes the story of the cow they were commanded to slaughter, which gives the surah its name. It recalls Ibrahim and Isma'il building the Ka'bah and the change of the qiblah from Jerusalem to the Ka'bah. It then sets out many laws for the new community: fasting, Hajj, marriage and divorce, charity, the ban on riba, and the writing of debts. It contains Ayat al-Kursi, which the Prophet ﷺ called the greatest ayah in the Quran (Sahih Muslim). He also said that whoever recites its last two ayahs at night, they will be enough for him (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
Holding firmly to Islam: the truth about Isa, and the lessons of the Battle of Uhud.

Aal-i-Imran is a Madinan surah revealed in stages. It declares that Allah sent down the Torah, the Injil and the Quran, and that the true religion with Allah is Islam. It tells the story of the family of Imran: the birth of Maryam, Zakariyya and his son Yahya, and the miraculous birth of Isa, whose creation without a father is likened to the creation of Adam. It invites the People of the Book to worship none but Allah. When the Christian delegation from Najran disputed about Isa, the Prophet ﷺ invited them to a mubahalah (a mutual call for Allah's curse on whoever was lying), and they declined (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). It urges the believers to hold together to the rope of Allah and not divide. A long part draws lessons from the Battle of Uhud, in the third year after the Hijrah: obedience, patience, and the honor of the martyrs. It ends with the reflection and prayers of people of understanding who ponder the creation of the heavens and the earth. The Prophet ﷺ said Al-Baqarah and Aal-i-Imran will come on the Day of Resurrection like two clouds, pleading for those who recited them (Sahih Muslim).
Justice and care in the family and society, especially for women, orphans and the weak.

An-Nisa is a Madinan surah revealed over several years as the Muslim community in Madinah took shape. It reminds all people that they were created from a single soul and must honor the ties of kinship. It protects the wealth of orphans and the dowry of women, sets out the shares of inheritance, explains whom one may marry, and teaches how to settle disputes between spouses. It commands worshipping Allah alone and kindness to parents, relatives, orphans and neighbors, returning trusts to their owners, judging with justice, and obeying Allah and His Messenger. It calls the believers to stand up for the oppressed, explains prayer while traveling and in fear, and commands justice even against oneself or one's parents. It exposes the hypocrites, and teaches that Isa was neither killed nor crucified, but Allah raised him to Himself. It states that Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but forgives anything less than that for whom He wills. When Ibn Mas'ud recited this surah to the Prophet ﷺ, the Prophet's eyes filled with tears (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
Fulfilling covenants with Allah, and the completion of the religion.

Al-Ma'idah is a late Madinan surah and among the last revealed. Its ayah "This day I have perfected your religion for you" was revealed on the Day of Arafah during the Farewell Hajj (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). It commands the believers to fulfil their contracts, sets out lawful and unlawful food, teaches wudu and tayammum, and commands justice even towards people one dislikes. It recalls the covenants of the Children of Israel and the Christians, and how Musa's people refused to enter the Holy Land. The story of Adam's two sons teaches that killing one soul unjustly is like killing all mankind. It describes the Quran as confirming and safeguarding the earlier scriptures, and rejects the claims that Allah is the Messiah or one of three. It sets rules on oaths, the final ban on wine and gambling, and hunting in ihram. It ends with the disciples asking Isa for a table of food from heaven, which gives the surah its name, and Isa's testimony that he only called people to worship Allah.
The Oneness of Allah and the rejection of idol worship and pagan customs.

Al-An'am is a Makkan surah that answers the Quraysh, who rejected the message, demanded miracles and held on to idol worship. It praises Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made darkness and light, and teaches that only He holds the keys of the unseen. It comforts the Prophet ﷺ in the face of rejection. It tells how Ibrahim reasoned with his people from the star, the moon and the sun to the worship of Allah alone, then names eighteen prophets whose guidance the Prophet ﷺ is told to follow. It points to Allah's signs in nature, and rejects the pagan customs of setting aside shares of crops and cattle for idols, forbidding animals without Allah's authority, and killing their children; these cattle give the surah its name. It sets out what Allah has truly forbidden, such as associating partners with Him and unjust killing, with commands to honor parents, deal fairly and keep promises. It ends with the declaration that one's prayer, sacrifice, life and death are all for Allah, Lord of the worlds.
Lessons from the stories of the prophets, and a warning against following Shaytan.

Al-A'raf is a Makkan surah that uses the stories of earlier prophets to warn those who rejected the Prophet ﷺ and to comfort the believers. It begins with the weighing of deeds on the Day of Judgment, then tells of Adam's creation, Iblis's refusal to prostrate and his vow to mislead people, and the repentance of Adam and his wife; the children of Adam are warned not to be deceived by Shaytan. It describes the people of Paradise and of the Fire calling to one another, with the people of the Heights between them, who give the surah its name. It tells of Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut and Shu'ayb and the destruction of the peoples who rejected them, and at greatest length of Musa with Pharaoh and the Children of Israel, including the golden calf. It recalls Allah's covenant with all of Adam's descendants, "Am I not your Lord?", teaches calling on Allah by His most beautiful names, and ends with listening to the Quran and remembering Allah humbly. Its last ayah is the first place of prostration in the order of the Quran.
The lessons of the Battle of Badr: victory comes from Allah.

Al-Anfal is a Madinan surah revealed about the Battle of Badr, the first major battle between the Muslims and the Quraysh, in the second year after the Hijrah (Sahih al-Bukhari). It begins by placing the spoils of war under Allah and His Messenger and describing the qualities of true believers. It recalls Badr: the reluctance of some believers, the angels Allah sent to help, the calm and rain He sent down, and that the victory came from Allah alone. It calls the believers to obey Allah and His Messenger and to answer him when he calls them to what gives them life, and recalls the plots of the Quraysh against the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah. It explains how the spoils are divided, teaches firmness, remembrance of Allah and unity in battle, and covers treaties, preparing strength, and accepting peace when the enemy inclines to it. It ends with the captives of Badr and the bonds between the Muhajirun, the Ansar and relatives. Its first ayah was revealed when Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas asked the Prophet ﷺ for a sword from the spoils (Sahih Muslim).
Exposing the hypocrites, and calling the believers to sincere repentance and sacrifice.

At-Tawbah, also called Bara'ah, is a late Madinan surah and among the last revealed (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). It is the only surah that does not begin with "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful". Much of it concerns the ninth year after the Hijrah: the expedition to Tabuk and the Hajj led by Abu Bakr, where its opening ayahs were proclaimed. It ends the treaties with the polytheists, while honoring treaties with those who kept them, and addresses the People of the Book and the sacred months. It calls the believers to march to Tabuk and recalls Allah's help to the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr in the cave. It names the eight groups who may receive zakah and exposes the excuses and mockery of the hypocrites, so much that Ibn Abbas called it "the Exposer" (Sahih al-Bukhari). It teaches that Allah has bought the believers' lives and wealth in return for Paradise, and tells how He accepted the repentance of the three who stayed behind from Tabuk, among them Ka'b ibn Malik (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). It ends with the Prophet's ﷺ deep care and mercy for the believers.
The truth of the revelation, and Allah's mercy to those who believe in time.

Yunus is a Makkan surah answering the Quraysh, who denied the revelation and the resurrection and found it strange that a man from among them should receive revelation. It points to Allah's power in creating the heavens and the earth, the sun and the moon, and shows how people call on Allah in hardship but turn away once He saves them. It likens worldly life to crops that flourish and then perish, and promises those who do good the best reward and more; the Prophet ﷺ explained the "more" as the people of Paradise seeing their Lord (Sahih Muslim). It challenges the deniers to produce a surah like the Quran, calls it a healing for what is in the hearts, and assures the friends of Allah that they will have no fear or grief. It tells of Nuh, and of Musa and Harun with Pharaoh, whose belief as he drowned came too late. It names the people of Yunus as the one town that believed in time and was spared the punishment, and ends by telling the Prophet ﷺ to follow the revelation and be patient until Allah judges.
Standing firm on the truth, as the earlier prophets did.

Hud is a late Makkan surah, revealed when the Quraysh were rejecting the Prophet ﷺ and opposing the believers. It calls people to worship Allah alone and seek His forgiveness, and challenges the deniers to produce ten surahs like the Quran. It then tells the stories of earlier prophets and their peoples: Nuh and the Flood, Hud and 'Ad, Salih and Thamud, Ibrahim and Lut, Shu'ayb and Madyan, and Musa and Pharaoh. In each, the messenger called his people to Allah, they rejected him, and the believers were saved. The surah commands the Prophet ﷺ to stand firm as he was commanded, not to lean towards wrongdoers, and to establish prayer, for good deeds remove bad deeds; this ayah was revealed when a man came to the Prophet ﷺ in remorse over a sin, and it applies to the whole ummah (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). These stories were told to strengthen the Prophet's ﷺ heart.
Patience, trust in Allah and forgiveness, through the story of Yusuf.

Yusuf is a late Makkan surah, and almost all of it tells one story, which Allah calls the best of stories. Yusuf dreams of eleven stars, the sun and the moon prostrating to him. His jealous brothers throw him into a well, and his father Ya'qub responds with beautiful patience. Sold in Egypt, Yusuf refuses the advances of his master's wife and chooses prison over sin. In prison he calls his fellow prisoners to worship Allah alone and interprets their dreams, then interprets the king's dream and is put in charge of the storehouses. When his brothers come for grain, the grieving Ya'qub tells his sons never to despair of Allah's mercy. Yusuf finally reveals himself and forgives his brothers, his father's sight is restored, and his dream comes true. The surah ends by calling these stories a lesson for people of understanding. The Prophet ﷺ described Yusuf as the noble son of the noble son of the noble son of the noble: Yusuf, son of Ya'qub, son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim (Sahih al-Bukhari).
Allah's signs in creation, the truth of the revelation, and the peace of remembering Allah.

Scholars differ on whether Ar-Ra'd was revealed in Makkah or Madinah. It points to Allah's signs: the heavens raised without visible pillars, the sun and moon, and gardens watered by the same water yet differing in taste. It answers those who deny the resurrection and describes Allah's complete knowledge, even of what every womb carries. It teaches that Allah does not change a people's condition until they change what is in themselves, and that even the thunder glorifies His praise. The parable of water and foam shows that truth remains while falsehood passes away. The people of understanding keep their covenant, join the ties of kinship, are patient, pray, spend and repel evil with good, and they will enter the Gardens of Eden. Hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah. The surah consoles the Prophet ﷺ, since earlier messengers were also mocked.
Gratitude to Allah, and the firm word of faith.

Ibrahim is a late Makkan surah, revealed when the Quraysh were rejecting the message and pressuring the believers. It teaches that the Book was sent to bring people out of darkness into light. Musa reminds his people that if they are grateful, Allah will give them more. Earlier messengers were threatened by their nations but relied on Allah, and on the Day of Judgment Shaytan will disown those who followed him. A good word is like a good tree with firm roots and branches in the sky, while an evil word is like an uprooted tree. Allah keeps the believers firm with the firm word, which the Prophet ﷺ explained as the questioning in the grave (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). Allah's favors cannot be counted. Ibrahim prays for Makkah to be safe, for himself and his children to be kept from idols, and for forgiveness for himself, his parents and the believers. The surah ends with warnings of the Day of Reckoning.
The preservation of the Quran, and lessons from nations who mocked their messengers.

Al-Hijr is a Makkan surah revealed when the disbelievers mocked the Prophet ﷺ and called him possessed. It states that Allah sent down the Reminder and will preserve it, and points to His signs in the sky, the earth and the winds. It tells of Adam's creation, Iblis's refusal to prostrate and his vow to mislead people, except Allah's sincere servants, and describes the reward of the righteous. The stories of Ibrahim's guests, the people of Lut, the People of the Wood and the people of al-Hijr (Thamud), who carved their homes in the mountains, follow. It ends by consoling the Prophet ﷺ: he has been given the seven oft-repeated ayahs, which he explained as Al-Fatihah (Sahih al-Bukhari), and the great Quran; he is told to proclaim the message openly and to worship his Lord until death comes.
Allah's countless blessings, and the duty to be grateful.

An-Nahl is a Makkan surah, mostly from the later Makkan period; some scholars hold that its last few ayahs were revealed in Madinah. It lists Allah's many blessings: livestock, rain and crops, night and day, the sea, the mountains and the stars, and says His favors cannot be counted. It answers those who called the revelation "tales of the ancients" and states that every nation was sent a messenger calling it to worship Allah and avoid false gods. It condemns the pagan custom of burying newborn daughters, and points to signs in milk, fruits and the bee, whose honey contains healing for people. It commands justice, excellence and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality, wrongdoing and oppression. Believers must keep their oaths, and a good life is promised to every believing man and woman who does righteous deeds. It presents Ibrahim as a model of devotion, and ends by commanding calling to Allah's way with wisdom, good advice and patience.
The Night Journey, and the commands that guide to what is most upright.

Al-Isra, also called Bani Isra'il, is a Makkan surah. It opens with the Night Journey, when Allah took the Prophet ﷺ by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, before the Hijrah. It recalls the corruption and punishment of the Children of Israel and describes the Quran as guiding to what is most upright. At its center is a set of commands: worship Allah alone, honor parents and do not even say "uff" to them, give relatives and the poor their due, avoid waste, do not kill children for fear of poverty, do not approach zina, keep promises and give full measure. It refutes shirk, affirms the resurrection, and tells the Prophet ﷺ to establish the prayers and pray at night, hoping for a praised station, which Sahih al-Bukhari explains as his intercession on the Day of Judgment. It declares that humans and jinn together could not produce the like of the Quran. At the conquest of Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ recited "Truth has come and falsehood has vanished" from this surah while striking down the idols around the Ka'bah (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
Four stories that teach holding firm to faith against the trials of this world.

Al-Kahf is a Makkan surah revealed when the Prophet ﷺ was grieved by his people's rejection and the believers faced pressure on their faith. It praises Allah for sending down a Book with no crookedness and warns those who claim Allah has a son. Four stories follow. The young men of the Cave left their people to protect their faith, and Allah made them sleep for many years. The owner of two gardens is ruined by pride in his wealth, showing that lasting good deeds are better than worldly adornment. Musa learns from a servant of Allah, named al-Khidr in Sahih al-Bukhari, whose actions hide a wisdom Musa could not see. Dhul-Qarnayn, a ruler given power on earth, builds a barrier against Ya'juj and Ma'juj. The surah ends: whoever hopes to meet his Lord should do righteous deeds and associate no one in His worship. Sahih Muslim reports that whoever memorizes its first ten ayahs will be protected from the Dajjal, and scholars such as al-Albani authenticated the hadith that reciting it on Friday brings light between the two Fridays.
Allah's mercy to His prophets, and the truth about Isa.

Maryam is a Makkan surah revealed during the persecution that led some Muslims to migrate to Abyssinia, where Ja'far ibn Abi Talib recited from its opening before the Najashi, and the king wept (Musnad Ahmad). It begins with Zakariyya's quiet prayer in old age and Allah's gift of his son Yahya. It tells how Maryam gave birth to Isa, and how the infant Isa spoke to defend her, declaring himself a servant of Allah and a prophet; it is not fitting for Allah to take a son. Ibrahim gently calls his father away from idols, followed by Musa, Harun, Isma'il and Idris, prophets who fell down in prostration, weeping, when Allah's ayahs were recited. Later generations neglected prayer, except those who repented. The surah answers those who deny the resurrection, warns that the claim that the Most Merciful has a son is so grave the heavens almost burst, and promises love from Allah for those who believe and do good.
The Quran as a reminder, taught through the story of Musa.

Ta-Ha is a Makkan surah. It opens by telling the Prophet ﷺ that the Quran was not sent down to cause him distress, but as a reminder for those who fear Allah. Most of the surah tells the story of Musa: Allah's call to him at the fire in the valley of Tuwa with the command to worship Him and establish prayer, his prayer for an expanded chest and for Harun as his helper, and Allah's care for him as a baby. Musa is told to speak gently to Pharaoh; the magicians believe and stand firm against Pharaoh's threats; the Children of Israel cross the sea; and al-Samiri leads them to worship a calf. The surah then describes the Day of Judgment and teaches the prayer "My Lord, increase me in knowledge". It tells how Adam was tempted by Iblis and how Allah accepted his repentance, and warns that whoever turns away from Allah's remembrance will have a hard life. It ends with patience, glorifying Allah, and commanding one's family to pray.
All the prophets brought one message: worship Allah alone.

Al-Anbiya is a Makkan surah that opens by warning that people's reckoning has drawn near while they turn away in heedlessness. The disbelievers call the Prophet ﷺ a poet or a sorcerer. Allah did not create the heavens and the earth in play, and if there were other gods besides Him, both would be ruined. Every living thing was made from water, and every soul will taste death. The surah recalls many prophets: Musa and Harun; Ibrahim, who broke the idols and was saved when the fire was made cool and safe for him; then Lut, Nuh, Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Isma'il, Idris, Dhul-Kifl, Yunus, Zakariyya, Yahya and Maryam. All of them called to the same truth and turned to Allah in hardship. The Prophet ﷺ said that no Muslim calls upon Allah with the prayer of Yunus, "There is no god but You, glory be to You; I have been among the wrongdoers", except that Allah answers him (Jami' al-Tirmidhi, authenticated by al-Albani). The surah ends with the Day when the heaven is rolled up like a scroll, and declares that the Prophet ﷺ was sent only as a mercy to the worlds.
The Hajj, sincere worship, and permission to defend the faith.

Scholars differ on whether Al-Hajj was revealed in Makkah or Madinah; many hold that it contains ayahs from both. It opens with the terrible earthquake of the Hour, and proves the resurrection from the stages of human creation and the reviving of dead earth. It describes those who worship Allah "on an edge", staying only while things go well. Ibrahim was told to purify the Sacred House and call people to Hajj, and the rites and sacrifices are set out: it is not their meat or blood that reaches Allah, but the piety of the believers. Believers driven from their homes only for saying "Our Lord is Allah" are given permission to fight back; Ibn Abbas said this was the first ayah permitting fighting (Jami' al-Tirmidhi). It teaches that it is not the eyes that are blind but the hearts, and that false gods could not create even a fly. Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim report that one of its ayahs was revealed about those who met in single combat at Badr. It ends by calling the believers to strive for Allah, who placed no hardship on them in religion, the faith of their father Ibrahim.
The qualities of the successful believers.

Al-Mu'minun is a Makkan surah revealed when the Quraysh were rejecting the message and mocking the believers. It opens with the qualities of the successful believers: they are humble in prayer, avoid idle talk, pay zakah, guard their chastity, keep their trusts and promises, and guard their prayers; they will inherit al-Firdaws. It describes the stages of human creation and resurrection and Allah's signs in nature. It recalls Nuh, later messengers, Musa and Harun, and Isa and his mother, all rejected by their peoples, while people split their one religion into sects. Allah alone owns and rules all things and has no son or partner. The surah teaches seeking refuge from the whispers of devils, describes the dying person who begs to return to do good, and the weighing of deeds. It asks, "Did you think We created you without purpose?", and ends with the prayer, "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, for You are the best of those who show mercy."
Purity, modesty, and protecting people's honor in the Muslim community.

An-Nur is a Madinan surah revealed after the slander against Aishah, the Mother of the Believers, on the return from the campaign against Banu al-Mustaliq. In Aishah's own account in Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim, Allah declared her innocence in this surah, and urged Abu Bakr to pardon his relative Mistah, who had spread the slander, after he had sworn to stop supporting him; Abu Bakr resumed his support. The surah sets out the punishment for zina and for accusing chaste women without four witnesses, and the oath procedure (li'an) between spouses. It teaches the believers to think well of one another and not to spread rumors. It gives the manners of entering homes, commands believing men and women to lower their gaze and guard their chastity, and encourages marriage. Its famous Ayah of Light describes Allah as the Light of the heavens and the earth. It promises the believers succession in the land, and ends with the manners of seeking permission.
The Quran as the criterion between truth and falsehood, and the servants of the Most Merciful.

Al-Furqan is a Makkan surah revealed when the Quraysh rejected the Quran as invented and mocked the Prophet ﷺ. It praises Allah, who sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan) as a warning to the worlds, and answers the claims that the Quran is invented and that a messenger should not eat food or walk in the markets. On the Day of Judgment the wrongdoer will bite his hands, wishing he had followed the Messenger rather than a misleading friend, and the Messenger will complain that his people abandoned the Quran. It recalls earlier nations and Allah's signs in nature. It closes with the qualities of the servants of the Most Merciful: they walk humbly, answer the ignorant with peace, pray at night, spend moderately, avoid shirk, unjust killing and zina, and pray for spouses and children who are a comfort to their eyes. Ibn Abbas reported that its promise to whoever repents, believes and does good, that Allah will replace his bad deeds with good ones, was revealed when some polytheists asked whether there was any way to make up for killing and zina (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
Comfort for the Prophet ﷺ through the stories of seven earlier messengers.

Ash-Shu'ara is a Makkan surah that opens by comforting the Prophet ﷺ, who was grieving deeply because his people would not believe. It tells seven stories of prophets and their peoples: Musa and Pharaoh; Ibrahim, who prayed not to be disgraced on the Day when neither wealth nor children help, except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart; Nuh; Hud; Salih; Lut; and Shu'ayb. Each story ends with the same refrain: in this is a sign, yet most of them did not believe, and your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful. The Quran was brought down by the Trustworthy Spirit, Jibril, in clear Arabic, not by devils. The Prophet ﷺ is told to warn his nearest relatives; when this was revealed, he climbed Mount al-Safa and called the clans of Quraysh to warn them (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). The surah ends by contrasting poets followed by the misguided with those who believe, do good and remember Allah often.
Gratitude for Allah's blessings, through the story of Sulayman.

An-Naml is a Makkan surah that opens by describing the Quran as guidance and good news for believers who pray, give zakah and are certain of the Hereafter. It recalls Musa's call and the nine signs that Pharaoh's people rejected though they were inwardly convinced. Most of the surah is about Dawud and Sulayman. Sulayman was taught the speech of birds; when an ant warned the other ants of his army, he smiled and prayed to be grateful for Allah's favors. The hoopoe brought news of the Queen of Saba, whose people worshipped the sun; Sulayman's letter to her began "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful", and the queen finally submitted with Sulayman to Allah. Brief stories of Salih and of Lut follow. The repeated question "Is there a god with Allah?" points to creation and to the One who answers the distressed when they call on Him. The surah teaches that only Allah knows the unseen, describes signs of the Hour, and ends with the command to worship the Lord of Makkah and recite the Quran.
Allah's support for the oppressed, through the life of Musa.

Al-Qasas is a late Makkan surah. Pharaoh oppressed the Children of Israel, but Allah willed to favor the oppressed. Musa's mother was inspired to place him in the river; Pharaoh's household took him in, and Allah returned him to his mother to nurse. As a young man Musa struck an Egyptian, who died from the blow; he sought Allah's forgiveness and fled to Madyan, where he helped two women water their flock, turned to Allah in his need, and married one of their father's daughters. At Mount Tur he was made a messenger and sent with Harun to Pharaoh, who was drowned with his army. The surah answers the excuses of the Makkans, and tells of Qarun, whose wealth made him arrogant until the earth swallowed him. Its ayah "You cannot guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills" was revealed about the Prophet's uncle Abu Talib, who died without accepting Islam (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). It ends: everything will perish except Allah's Face.
Faith is tested, and true protection is with Allah alone.

Al-'Ankabut is a Makkan surah according to most scholars, revealed during a time of severe persecution; some hold that its opening ayahs were revealed in Madinah. It asks whether people think they will be left to say "We believe" without being tested, for trials show who is truthful. Believers must be kind to their parents, but not obey them in associating partners with Allah. It recalls Nuh, who lived among his people for nine hundred and fifty years, Ibrahim and Lut, Shu'ayb, 'Ad and Thamud, and Qarun, Pharaoh and Haman, each seized for their sins. Those who take protectors other than Allah are like the spider, whose house is the weakest of houses. Prayer restrains from immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater. Allah's earth is spacious and He provides for every creature. Worldly life is only play, while the Hereafter is the true life, and Allah will guide those who strive for His sake.
Allah's promise always comes true, and His signs in creation.

Ar-Rum is a Makkan surah revealed after the Persians had defeated the Byzantine Romans. The polytheists of Makkah favored the Persians, while the Muslims favored the Romans as People of the Book (Jami' al-Tirmidhi). The surah foretold that the Romans would be victorious within a few years, and this came true. It teaches that people know only the outward side of worldly life and are heedless of the Hereafter. A series of "among His signs" passages follows: humans created from dust, spouses created for tranquility with affection and mercy between them, the variety of languages and colors, sleep, lightning and rain. People are told to turn to the true religion, the natural disposition (fitrah) on which Allah created them; the Prophet ﷺ said that every child is born upon the fitrah (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). Riba does not increase with Allah, while zakah given for His sake is multiplied. Corruption appears on land and sea because of what people's hands have earned. It ends by telling the Prophet ﷺ to be patient, for Allah's promise is true.
Wisdom and good character, through Luqman's advice to his son.

Luqman is a Makkan surah revealed while the Quraysh were turning people away from the Quran and holding on to the ways of their forefathers. It describes the Quran as guidance and mercy for those who do good, in contrast to those who buy idle talk to lead people away from Allah's path. At its center is the wisdom Allah gave Luqman and his advice to his son: do not associate partners with Allah, for that is a great wrong; be good to parents but do not obey them in shirk; know that Allah will bring forth even a deed the weight of a mustard seed; pray, command good, forbid evil and be patient; and avoid arrogance, walk modestly and lower your voice. It reminds people of Allah's favors, criticizes blind following of forefathers, and says that if every tree were a pen and the sea were ink, Allah's words would not run out. It ends by warning of a Day when no parent can help a child, and names five things known only to Allah: the Hour, the coming of rain, what is in the wombs, what a soul will earn tomorrow, and in what land it will die. The Prophet ﷺ called these five "the keys of the unseen" (Sahih al-Bukhari).
The truth of the Quran and the resurrection, and the humility of true believers.

As-Sajdah is a Makkan surah answering those who called the Quran a forgery and denied the resurrection. It affirms that the Book is from the Lord of the worlds, beyond doubt, and describes Allah creating the heavens and the earth in six days and directing every affair, and creating man from clay, then from a drop of fluid, then shaping him and breathing into him of His spirit. The deniers are told that the angel of death will take them, and the guilty will hang their heads before their Lord, begging to be sent back. True believers fall into prostration when reminded, leave their beds at night to call on their Lord in fear and hope, and spend from what He gave them; no soul knows the joy kept hidden for them. A believer and a defiant sinner are not equal. It recalls the Book given to Musa, and ends with the lesson of destroyed nations and of rain reviving dead land. The Prophet ﷺ used to recite this surah with Al-Insan in the Fajr prayer on Friday (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
The lessons of the Battle of the Trench, and the honor of the Prophet's ﷺ household.

Al-Ahzab is a Madinan surah, much of it revealed around the Battle of the Trench in 5 AH, when the Quraysh and their allies (al-Ahzab, "the Confederates") besieged Madinah and the Jewish tribe of Banu Qurayzah broke its treaty with the Prophet ﷺ. It ends the custom of treating adopted sons as real sons; this came while Zayd ibn Harithah was still being called "Zayd ibn Muhammad" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). It describes the siege, when hearts reached the throats: the hypocrites' excuses, the believers who stayed true to their covenant, the Prophet ﷺ as the best example, and Allah turning the Confederates back. It addresses the Prophet's wives, who chose Allah and His Messenger, lists the qualities of believing men and women, and states that Muhammad ﷺ is the Seal of the Prophets. It calls for much remembrance of Allah, gives manners for the Prophet's homes, including the ayah of hijab, commands sending blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, and instructs believing women about their outer garments. It ends with the Trust that the heavens, the earth and the mountains declined, and man took on.
Gratitude versus ingratitude for Allah's favors.

Saba is a Makkan surah answering those who denied the Hour and called the Prophet ﷺ a liar or mad. It praises Allah, whose knowledge misses not even an atom's weight, and affirms that the Hour will come. It contrasts two responses to Allah's favors. Dawud and Sulayman, given power over iron, the wind and the jinn, remained grateful; the jinn did not even know of Sulayman's death until a creature of the earth ate through his staff. The people of Saba, given two gardens, turned away and were struck by a flood that ruined their gardens and scattered them. The surah challenges the idolaters: their gods own nothing, and no intercession helps except with Allah's permission. The Prophet ﷺ is sent to all mankind, and wealth and children do not bring anyone closer to Allah, only faith and righteous deeds; whatever is spent for His sake He replaces. It ends by urging people to stand up for Allah, in pairs or alone, and reflect that their companion is not mad but a warner before a severe punishment.
Allah the Creator, on whom all creation depends.

Fatir is a Makkan surah that comforts the Prophet ﷺ in the face of rejection and calls people to the One Creator. It praises Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who makes the angels messengers with wings, and whose mercy no one can hold back. Earlier messengers were also denied, so people should not be deceived by worldly life or by Shaytan, who is a clear enemy. Winds, rain, the creation of man and the two seas show Allah's power to raise the dead. People are in need of Allah, while He is free of all needs, and no soul will carry another's burden. From the varied colors of fruits, mountains, people and animals, it teaches that those of His servants who truly fear Allah are those with knowledge. Those who recite the Book, pray and spend hope for a trade that will never fail, and the inheritors of the Book are of three kinds: those who wrong themselves, those in between, and those foremost in good deeds. It ends with a reminder that if Allah punished people at once for their deeds, He would not leave a single creature on the earth.
The truth of the Prophet's ﷺ message, and the certainty of the resurrection.

Ya-Sin is a Makkan surah. It swears by the wise Quran that the Prophet ﷺ is one of the messengers on a straight path, sent to warn a people whose forefathers were not warned, and states that Allah records people's deeds and the traces they leave behind. It tells of a town that rejected the messengers sent to it; a man came running from the far end of the town urging his people to follow them, was told to enter Paradise, and wished his people knew how his Lord had forgiven him, while they were destroyed by a single cry. Signs follow: dead land brought to life, pairs in creation, night and day, the sun running its course, the phases of the moon, each floating in its orbit, and ships on the sea. It describes the blowing of the trumpet, the joy of the people of Paradise greeted with "Peace" from a Merciful Lord, and the guilty whose mouths are sealed while their hands and feet testify. It ends by answering those who doubt that crumbled bones can live again: the One who created them the first time will give them life, for when He wills a thing, He only says "Be", and it is.
The Oneness of Allah, and the victory of His messengers.

As-Saffat is a Makkan surah affirming the Oneness of Allah against the idolaters' claims about the angels and the jinn. It swears by the angels standing in ranks that your God is One, and describes the stars that adorn and guard the lowest heaven. It answers the deniers of the resurrection with a scene of the Judgment, where the misled and their leaders blame each other, while one of Allah's sincere servants in Paradise looks down to see his former companion in the Fire. It then recounts the prophets: Nuh; Ibrahim, who broke his people's idols, then saw in a dream that he was sacrificing his son, who submitted, until Allah ransomed him with a great sacrifice; Musa and Harun; Ilyas; Lut; and Yunus, swallowed by the fish and saved because he glorified Allah. It refutes the claim that the angels are Allah's daughters, promises victory to Allah's messengers and His soldiers, and ends by glorifying Allah and sending peace on the messengers.
Pride leads to rejection, while the prophets turned to Allah in repentance.

Sad is a Makkan surah revealed while the leaders of Quraysh were rejecting the call to worship One God out of pride. It describes their amazement that a warner came from among them and made "the gods one God", and recalls earlier nations who denied, from the people of Nuh to Pharaoh. Then come the prophets: Dawud, with whom the mountains and birds glorified Allah, who sought his Lord's forgiveness and was made a ruler to judge with truth; Sulayman, granted a kingdom like no one after him; and Ayyub, whose patience in illness and loss was rewarded with relief and the return of his family; along with Ibrahim, Ishaq, Ya'qub, Isma'il, al-Yasa' and Dhul-Kifl. It says the Book was sent down, blessed, so that people reflect on its ayahs. After contrasting Paradise and the Fire, it tells how Iblis refused out of pride to prostrate to Adam, was expelled, and swore to mislead all except Allah's sincere servants. The Prophet ﷺ prostrated when reciting this surah (Sahih al-Bukhari).
Sincere worship of Allah, and never despairing of His mercy.

Az-Zumar is a Makkan surah calling people to worship Allah sincerely, devoting their religion to Him alone. It rejects the idolaters' excuse that they worship others only to be brought nearer to Allah, and shows His power in creating the heavens and the earth, night and day, and man in stages in the womb. People call on Allah in hardship and forget Him in ease, yet those who know and those who do not know are not equal, and the patient will receive their reward without measure. Allah has sent down the best of speech, a Book that makes the skins of those who fear Him shiver. Its well-known call to Allah's servants who have wronged themselves not to despair of His mercy, for He forgives all sins, was revealed when people who had killed and committed adultery asked whether there was any way to make up for it (Sahih al-Bukhari); it is followed by the call to turn back to Allah before punishment comes. It ends with the Day of Resurrection, when people are driven in groups to the Fire or led in groups to Paradise, whose gates open to greet them with peace.
Allah forgives and accepts repentance, and He defends the believers.

Ghafir, also called al-Mu'min ("the Believer"), is a Makkan surah and the first of the seven surahs that open with Ha Mim. It was revealed as the Quraysh argued against Allah's signs and opposed the Prophet ﷺ. It introduces Allah as the Forgiver of sin, the Accepter of repentance, and severe in punishment. The angels who carry the Throne glorify Allah and ask forgiveness for the believers. The longest part tells of Musa and Pharaoh, and of a believing man from Pharaoh's family who hid his faith, asked "Will you kill a man for saying my Lord is Allah?", warned his people, and entrusted his affair to Allah, who protected him. Abu Bakr used these same words when he pushed away a man who was choking the Prophet ﷺ at the Ka'bah (Sahih al-Bukhari). Allah promises to support His messengers and the believers, and says "Call upon Me; I will answer you"; the Prophet ﷺ recited this after saying that supplication is worship (Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, graded authentic). It ends with a warning that faith declared only on seeing the punishment brings no benefit.
The Quran explained in detail, and steadfastness in calling to Allah.

Fussilat, also called Ha Mim as-Sajdah, is a Makkan surah revealed while the Quraysh were trying to stop people from listening to the Quran. It presents the Quran as a Book explained in detail in clear Arabic, while most turn away saying their hearts are covered. It describes the creation of the earth and the heavens, and warns of a punishment like the one that struck 'Ad and Thamud. On the Day of Judgment the enemies of Allah will find their own hearing, sight and skins testifying against them; Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim report that this was revealed when some men at the Ka'bah wondered whether Allah hears what they say. Those who say "Our Lord is Allah" and remain steadfast will be told by the angels not to fear or grieve. None is better in speech than one who calls to Allah, and evil should be repelled with good, which can turn an enemy into a close friend. The sun and moon are signs, so prostrate to Allah alone. It ends: Allah will show people His signs in the horizons and within themselves until it is clear that this is the truth.
One religion for all the prophets, and the qualities of the believers, including consultation.

Ash-Shura is a Makkan surah stressing that the message of the Prophet ﷺ is the same religion given to all the prophets. It opens with the revelation from Allah, at whose majesty the heavens almost burst apart, while the angels glorify Him and ask forgiveness for those on earth. Nothing is like Allah, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing. The same religion was ordained for Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad ﷺ: establish it and do not divide in it. Allah accepts repentance, and whatever misfortune strikes is because of what people's hands have earned, though He pardons much. The believers rely on their Lord, avoid major sins, forgive when angry, establish prayer, run their affairs by mutual consultation (shura), spend, and defend themselves when wronged, while pardoning is better. Allah gives daughters, sons, both or none as He wills, and speaks to human beings only through inspiration, from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger. It ends by describing the Quran as a spirit by His command that guides to a straight path.
The smallness of worldly wealth compared with faith and the Hereafter.

Az-Zukhruf is a Makkan surah answering the idolaters who followed their forefathers blindly, called the angels Allah's daughters, and judged people's worth by wealth. It affirms that the Arabic Quran is recorded with Allah in the Mother of the Book, and reminds the idolaters that they themselves admit Allah created the heavens and the earth. It teaches the words to say when riding, which the Prophet ﷺ used in his supplication for travel (Sahih Muslim). It condemns the excuse "we found our fathers on a way", while Ibrahim declared himself free of what his people worshipped. To the objection that the Quran should have come to a great man of Makkah or Ta'if, it replies that Allah apportions livelihood, and that worldly silver and gold ornaments (zukhruf) are small compared with the Hereafter, which is for the righteous. It tells of Pharaoh boasting of his rivers and mocking Musa, and states that Isa was a servant whom Allah favored. Close friends will become enemies on that Day, except the righteous. It ends by affirming that Allah has no son and that He is God in the heavens and on earth.
A warning to the deniers, and the blessed night in which the Quran was sent down.

Ad-Dukhan is a Makkan surah revealed during the years when the Quraysh persisted in rejecting the Prophet ﷺ. It begins by stating that the Quran was sent down in a blessed night, in which every matter of wisdom is decreed. It warns of a day when the sky will bring a visible smoke covering the people. Ibn Mas'ud reported that when the Quraysh resisted the Prophet ﷺ, he prayed for years of famine against them, until hunger made them see something like smoke between the sky and the earth; they asked him to pray for relief, and these ayahs were revealed (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). Other Companions and scholars understood the smoke as one of the major signs before the Hour. It tells how Pharaoh's people rejected Musa and were drowned, leaving behind gardens, springs and fine dwellings, and neither heaven nor earth wept for them. It answers those who deny the resurrection, describes the tree of Zaqqum as the food of the sinful, and describes the security and gardens of the righteous, who will taste no death after the first death.
Reflecting on Allah's signs, and the Day every nation kneels before Him.

Al-Jathiyah is a Makkan surah calling people to reflect on Allah's signs and warning those who mock them. It points to signs in the heavens and the earth, in the creation of people and animals, in night and day, rain and the winds, and warns every sinful liar who hears Allah's ayahs and turns away in arrogance. Allah has made the sea and all that is in the heavens and the earth of service to people, and the believers are told to forgive those who do not expect the days of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ is placed on a clear path and must follow it, not people's desires. It condemns the one who takes his own desires as his god, and those who say only time destroys them; in a hadith qudsi, Allah says that the son of Adam wrongs Him by cursing time, while it is He who turns the night and the day (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). On the Day of Judgment every nation will be seen kneeling, called to its record. It ends in praise of Allah, Lord of the heavens and the earth, to whom belongs all greatness.
The truth of the Quran, kindness to parents, and the lesson of 'Ad.

Al-Ahqaf is a Makkan surah, the last of the seven Ha Mim surahs, answering those who called the Quran magic or a forgery. It declares that the heavens and the earth were created with truth, and that the idols created nothing and will deny their worshippers on the Day of Judgment. The Prophet ﷺ is told to say that he is not the first of the messengers and only follows what is revealed to him, and that the Quran confirms the Book of Musa. It commands kindness to parents, recalling the mother's hardship in pregnancy and nursing, and gives the prayer of one who reaches forty years. It recalls Hud warning his people 'Ad among the sand dunes (al-Ahqaf); seeing a cloud, they thought it would bring rain, but it was a wind carrying a painful punishment. Because of this, the Prophet ﷺ would become anxious whenever he saw clouds (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). A group of jinn listened to the Quran, believed, and went back to warn their people. It ends by telling the Prophet ﷺ to be patient, as the messengers of firm resolve were patient.
Striving in Allah's cause, and exposing the hypocrites.

Muhammad, also called al-Qital ("Fighting"), is a Madinan surah revealed after fighting in Allah's cause had been prescribed, when the Muslims faced the hostility of the Quraysh and the wavering of the hypocrites. Allah makes the deeds of those who disbelieve and block His path go to waste, while He forgives the believers and sets their affairs right. It gives instructions for battle and captives, promises that the deeds of those killed in Allah's cause will not be lost, and assures the believers that if they support Allah, He will support them and make their feet firm. It describes the rivers of Paradise, of pure water, milk, delicious wine and purified honey. It commands knowing that there is no god but Allah and seeking forgiveness. The hypocrites fear death when fighting is commanded, and are warned against spreading corruption and cutting the ties of kinship; Abu Hurayrah recited these ayahs with the hadith in which kinship seeks Allah's protection from being cut (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). It asks, "Do they not reflect on the Quran, or are there locks on their hearts?", and ends: if they turn away, Allah will replace them with another people.
The Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah as a clear victory.

Al-Fath is a Madinan surah revealed in 6 AH on the way back from al-Hudaybiyah. The Prophet ﷺ had set out for 'Umrah with about 1,400 Companions; the Quraysh blocked them, and a treaty was signed whose terms seemed hard to many Muslims. On the journey home, the Prophet ﷺ said that a surah had been revealed to him that night which was dearer to him than everything the sun rises over (Sahih al-Bukhari). Allah calls the treaty a clear victory, through which He forgives the Prophet ﷺ, completes His favor on him, and sends tranquility into the believers' hearts. Those who pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ were pledging to Allah, while the Bedouins who stayed behind with false excuses are exposed. Allah was pleased with the believers who pledged under the tree, and the Prophet ﷺ said none of them would enter the Fire, if Allah wills (Sahih Muslim). Allah confirmed the Prophet's dream of entering the Sacred Mosque in safety, and promised that His religion will prevail. It ends by describing the Companions as firm against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves, and marked by prostration.
Manners towards Allah, His Messenger and fellow believers.

Al-Hujurat is a Madinan surah from the later years, when delegations of Arab tribes were coming to the Prophet ﷺ. It teaches the believers not to put themselves before Allah and His Messenger or raise their voices above the Prophet's voice; Sahih al-Bukhari reports this was revealed after Abu Bakr and Umar raised their voices disagreeing over who should lead the Banu Tamim delegation. News brought by a sinful person must be verified before acting on it. If two groups of believers fight, peace must be made between them with justice, for the believers are brothers. Believers must not mock one another, insult one another or use offensive nicknames, and must avoid much suspicion, spying and backbiting, which is likened to eating a dead brother's flesh. All people were created from one male and one female and made into nations and tribes to know one another, and the most honored in Allah's sight is the most righteous. It ends by telling Bedouins who claimed faith to say rather "we have submitted", since faith had not yet entered their hearts.
The certainty of resurrection, and Allah's knowledge of every thought and word.

Qaf is a Makkan surah answering the disbelievers' amazement at the idea of being raised after becoming dust. It replies that Allah knows exactly what the earth takes from them, and all is kept in a preserved record. The sky built without flaws, the earth spread out with mountains and plants, and rain bringing dead land to life show how the dead will come forth, and earlier nations who denied their messengers met their fate. Allah knows even what a person's soul whispers to him, and two recording angels note every word he says. Then come the agony of death, the blowing of the trumpet, and each soul brought with a driver and a witness. Hell is asked whether it is full and replies "Are there more?", while Paradise is brought near to those who feared the Most Merciful unseen. It ends with a command to be patient and glorify Allah, and to remind with the Quran whoever fears Allah's warning. The Prophet ﷺ recited this surah on Fridays from the pulpit and in the Eid prayers (Sahih Muslim).
The Day of Recompense is certain, and mankind was created to worship Allah.

Adh-Dhariyat is a Makkan surah affirming that the Day of Recompense is certain. It swears by the scattering winds, the rain-bearing clouds, the gliding ships and the angels who distribute by Allah's command that the promise is true and judgment will come. Those who deny it are lost in confusion, while the righteous slept little at night, sought forgiveness before dawn, and gave the one who asks and the deprived their due. There are signs on the earth and within people themselves, and their provision is in the heaven. The angels came as guests to Ibrahim with glad tidings of a knowledgeable son, then went to destroy the people of Lut, sparing the one house of Muslims; Musa and Pharaoh, 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Nuh are further lessons. Allah created everything in pairs, so flee to Allah. Every messenger was called a magician or a madman, but reminding benefits the believers. It ends: Allah created jinn and mankind only to worship Him; He wants no provision from them, for He is the Provider.
Allah's punishment will surely come, and the reward of the righteous.

At-Tur is a Makkan surah. It swears by Mount Tur, the written Book, the much-visited House, the raised canopy of the sky and the filled sea that the punishment of your Lord will come and none can repel it, on a day when the sky sways and the mountains move. The righteous enjoy gardens and companions, and their believing offspring will be joined with them without any loss to their own reward. The Prophet ﷺ is told to keep reminding, for he is neither a soothsayer nor a madman, and a series of questions confronts the disbelievers: were they created from nothing, or are they the creators, and did they create the heavens and the earth? It ends by telling the Prophet ﷺ to be patient, for he is under Allah's watchful care, and to glorify his Lord when he rises, at night and as the stars fade. Jubayr ibn Mut'im, before he became Muslim, heard the Prophet ﷺ recite this surah in the Maghrib prayer, and said that was when faith first settled in his heart (Sahih al-Bukhari).
The truth of the revelation, and the falsehood of idols.

An-Najm is an early Makkan surah, and the first surah with a prostration to be revealed. The Prophet ﷺ recited it in Makkah and prostrated, and everyone present prostrated with him, Muslims and idolaters, except one man (Sahih al-Bukhari). It swears that the Prophet ﷺ has not gone astray and does not speak from his own desire; it is revelation taught to him by Jibril, whom he saw on the highest horizon and again at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, where he saw some of the greatest signs of his Lord. It exposes the idols al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat as mere names, condemns calling the angels Allah's daughters, and states that no intercession helps except with Allah's permission. Those who avoid major sins and shameful deeds, apart from small faults, will find their Lord vast in forgiveness. Recalling the scriptures of Musa and Ibrahim, it teaches that no one will carry another's burden, that each person will have only what he strove for, and that the final return is to Allah. It ends by warning that the Hour has drawn near, and commands prostration and worship of Allah.
The splitting of the moon, and the lessons of nations who denied their warners.

Al-Qamar is a Makkan surah revealed after the splitting of the moon: the people of Makkah asked the Prophet ﷺ for a sign and were shown the moon split in two (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). It opens: the Hour has drawn near and the moon has split, yet the disbelievers turn away and call every sign passing magic. It then recounts the destruction of those who denied their warners: the people of Nuh, 'Ad, Thamud, who killed the she-camel, the people of Lut, and Pharaoh's people. After each story comes the repeated reminder that Allah has made the Quran easy to remember, so is there anyone who will take heed? It warns that the gathered disbelievers will be defeated and turn their backs, which the Prophet ﷺ recited at Badr (Sahih al-Bukhari). It teaches that Allah created everything according to a measure (qadar), revealed when the Quraysh came disputing with the Prophet ﷺ about qadar (Sahih Muslim). It ends with the righteous among gardens and rivers, in a seat of honor near the All-Powerful King.
The countless favors of the Most Merciful to mankind and jinn.

Scholars differ on whether Ar-Rahman was revealed in Makkah or Madinah; most classical commentators, including Ibn Kathir, consider it Makkan. It addresses both mankind and jinn, asking again and again, "Which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?", a refrain repeated 31 times. The Most Merciful taught the Quran, created man and taught him clear speech. The sun and moon run by precise measure, the plants and trees prostrate to Him, and He set up the balance so that people would not cheat. He created man from clay and the jinn from smokeless fire, and made the two seas meet with a barrier between them, yielding pearls and coral. Everyone on earth will perish, and only the Face of your Lord, full of Majesty and Honor, remains. For those who feared standing before their Lord there are two gardens, and besides them two more, for the reward of good is nothing but good. The Prophet ﷺ described two gardens of silver and two of gold (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
The Day of Resurrection, and the three groups of people.

Al-Waqi'ah is a Makkan surah describing the Day of Resurrection and the three groups into which people will be divided. When the inevitable Event comes, no one will deny it; it will bring some low and raise others. People will be in three groups: the foremost, who are brought nearest to Allah; the people of the right; and the people of the left. The foremost and the people of the right enjoy the blessings of Paradise, where, the Prophet ﷺ said, there is a tree in whose shade a rider could travel for a hundred years (Sahih al-Bukhari). The people of the left suffer scorching wind, boiling water and the tree of Zaqqum, for they lived in luxury, persisted in great sin and denied the resurrection. Allah's creation of man, the crops, the rain and fire are proofs of His power to raise the dead. Allah swears by the positions of the stars that this is a noble Quran; Sahih Muslim reports this was revealed when some people credited rain to the stars rather than to Allah. It ends with the moment of death, when no one can return the soul, and the fate of each group.
Deepening faith, and spending in Allah's cause.

Al-Hadid is a Madinan surah, according to most scholars, urging the believers to deepen their faith and spend in Allah's cause. Everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah, the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, who is with people wherever they are. Believers are called to spend from what Allah has entrusted to them; those who spent and fought before the victory are higher in rank than those who did so after, though Allah has promised good to all. On the Day of Judgment the believers' light will run before them, while the hypocrites beg to borrow from it and are shut out by a wall. It asks whether the time has not come for the believers' hearts to be humbled by the remembrance of Allah, and compares worldly life to plants that flourish after rain and then dry up. Every misfortune is written before it happens, so that people neither despair over what they missed nor exult over what they gained. Allah sent His messengers with the Book and the balance so that people would uphold justice, and sent down iron with great strength and benefits.
Allah hears every plea, and the true loyalty of the believers.

Al-Mujadilah is a Madinan surah named after "the woman who pleaded". Khawlah bint Tha'labah came to the Prophet ﷺ complaining that her husband had declared zihar on her (saying "you are to me like my mother's back"), and Allah revealed its opening. Aishah, who was in the same room yet could not hear all of the woman's words, praised Allah whose hearing encompasses all voices (Sunan al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah). The surah declares such words false and wrong, and sets out their expiation. Allah knows every private conversation: there is no secret talk of three but He is the fourth of them. Secret talk for sin is forbidden, and the believers are told to make room for one another in gatherings; Allah raises in rank those who believe and those given knowledge. It condemns the hypocrites who befriend a people with whom Allah is angry and swear false oaths, and ends by stating that true believers will not love those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even close relatives; they are the party of Allah, who will succeed.
The expulsion of Banu al-Nadir, the generosity of the Ansar, and Allah's beautiful names.

Al-Hashr is a Madinan surah revealed about the expulsion of the Jewish tribe of Banu al-Nadir from Madinah after they broke their covenant with the Prophet ﷺ; Ibn Abbas called it "the surah of Banu al-Nadir" (Sahih al-Bukhari). Allah drove them out of the strong fortresses they thought would protect them, so let those with insight take a lesson. It explains that wealth gained without fighting goes to those in need, so that it does not circulate only among the rich, and teaches: whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, avoid it. It praises the poor emigrants, the Ansar who preferred others over themselves even when in need, and those who came after them praying for their brothers in faith; the praise of the Ansar was revealed about an Ansari couple who fed a guest of the Prophet ﷺ while their own children went to sleep hungry (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). The hypocrites promised Banu al-Nadir help and then abandoned them. It tells the believers to look at what they have sent ahead for tomorrow, and ends with some of Allah's most beautiful names.
Loyalty to Allah, and fairness to those who do not fight the Muslims.

Al-Mumtahanah is a Madinan surah revealed between the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah and the conquest of Makkah. It opens by forbidding the believers to take Allah's enemies as allies and show them affection. This was revealed about Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, a Companion who fought at Badr, who secretly wrote to the Quraysh about the Prophet's preparations to march on Makkah, hoping to protect his family there; the letter was intercepted, and the Prophet ﷺ accepted his excuse (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). Ibrahim and those with him are an excellent example in disowning their people's idol worship. Allah may yet put affection between the believers and their enemies, and He does not forbid kindness and justice towards those who have not fought them or driven them from their homes. Believing women who emigrate are to be examined, which gives the surah its name, and if found sincere they are not to be returned to the disbelievers. It sets out the pledge of the believing women to the Prophet ﷺ.
Matching words with deeds, and striving for Allah's religion.

As-Saff is a Madinan surah. Some Companions said that if they knew which deed Allah loves most, they would do it; Allah then revealed this surah, and the Prophet ﷺ recited it to them (al-Tirmidhi and Ahmad, graded sahih by al-Albani). It rebukes those who say what they do not do, and declares that Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row as if they were a solid structure. Musa's people hurt him though they knew he was Allah's messenger, and Isa gave glad tidings of a messenger to come after him named Ahmad. The disbelievers want to put out Allah's light with their mouths, but Allah will complete His light and make His religion prevail. It points the believers to a trade that saves from a painful punishment: believing in Allah and His Messenger and striving with wealth and lives, rewarded with forgiveness, Paradise and a near victory. It ends by calling the believers to be helpers of Allah, as the disciples of Isa were.
The blessing of the Prophet's ﷺ mission, and the Friday prayer.

Al-Jumu'ah is a Madinan surah. Allah sent among the unlettered people a Messenger from among them, who recites His ayahs to them, purifies them and teaches them the Book and wisdom, and also to others who would come later; when asked who these others are, the Prophet ﷺ placed his hand on Salman al-Farisi and said that even if faith were at the Pleiades, men from his people would reach it (Sahih al-Bukhari). Those given the Torah who did not act on it are likened to a donkey carrying books. When the call to prayer is made on Friday, the believers are told to hurry to the remembrance of Allah and leave trade, then disperse and seek Allah's bounty after the prayer. Its last ayah was revealed when a trade caravan arrived during the Friday sermon and people left until only twelve men remained with the Prophet ﷺ (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). The Prophet ﷺ used to recite this surah and Al-Munafiqun in the Friday prayer (Sahih Muslim).
The signs of the hypocrites, and not letting wealth distract from Allah.

Al-Munafiqun is a Madinan surah exposing the hypocrites. During a campaign, identified in the sirah as the expedition against Banu al-Mustaliq, Abdullah ibn Ubayy, leader of the hypocrites, told his followers not to spend on those with the Prophet ﷺ so that they would leave him, and said that on returning to Madinah the more honored would drive out the more humble. The young Companion Zayd ibn Arqam reported this; Ibn Ubayy swore he had not said it, until Allah revealed this surah confirming Zayd (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). The hypocrites testify that Muhammad is Allah's Messenger, but Allah testifies that they are liars; they use their oaths as a shield and have fine speech, but they are the real enemy. Their words are answered: honor belongs to Allah, His Messenger and the believers. It ends by warning the believers not to let wealth and children distract them from the remembrance of Allah, and to spend before death comes and a person wishes for a short delay to give charity.
The Day of mutual loss and gain, and trust in Allah through trials.

Most scholars consider At-Taghabun Madinan, though some said it is Makkan. Everything glorifies Allah, who created people, some believing and some disbelieving, and who knows what they hide and reveal. Earlier nations rejected their messengers and were punished. The disbelievers claim they will not be raised, but the Prophet ﷺ is told to swear by his Lord that they will be; the Day of Gathering is the Day of mutual loss and gain (at-Taghabun), when the believers win Paradise and the deniers lose. No misfortune happens except by Allah's permission, and whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart. Some spouses and children can be enemies to a believer by holding him back from obeying Allah, yet he is urged to pardon and forgive, for wealth and children are a trial; al-Tirmidhi reports this was revealed about men in Makkah whose families stopped them from emigrating to the Prophet ﷺ. It ends: fear Allah as much as you are able, listen, obey and spend, for whoever is saved from his own greed is successful.
The rules of divorce, built on mindfulness of Allah and fairness.

At-Talaq is a Madinan surah setting out the rules of divorce with constant reminders of taqwa (mindfulness of Allah); Ibn Mas'ud called it "the shorter Surah an-Nisa" (Sahih al-Bukhari). It instructs that divorce be given at its proper time with the waiting period ('iddah) counted, and that women not be put out of their homes during it. At the end of the term, the husband either keeps her on good terms or parts on good terms, with two just witnesses. Among these rulings come its well-known promises: whoever fears Allah, He will make a way out for him and provide for him from where he does not expect; whoever relies on Allah, He is enough for him; and Allah will bring ease after hardship. It covers housing, maintenance and nursing, each according to one's means. It warns of towns that rebelled against Allah's command, and ends with Allah's creation of seven heavens and of the earth like them, so that people know His power and knowledge encompass all things.
Lessons from the Prophet's ﷺ household, sincere repentance, and examples of true faith.

At-Tahrim is a Madinan surah concerning events in the household of the Prophet ﷺ. According to Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim, its opening came after the Prophet ﷺ swore not to drink honey again, following an arrangement between two of his wives. Allah asks the Prophet ﷺ why he forbids himself what Allah has made lawful, and states that He has prescribed a way to release oneself from oaths. A secret the Prophet ﷺ told one of his wives was disclosed, and the two wives are called to repent. The believers are told to protect themselves and their families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones, and are called to sincere repentance. The surah ends with examples: the wives of Nuh and Lut, whom their husbands' status could not save, and the wife of Pharaoh and Maryam daughter of Imran, models of true faith.
Allah's complete sovereignty, and life as a test.

Al-Mulk is a Makkan surah reminding the idolaters of Allah's complete sovereignty and warning those who denied the resurrection. Allah, in whose hand is all dominion, created death and life to test who is best in deeds, and built seven heavens without any flaw. The disbelievers will be thrown into Hell and confess that, had they listened or reasoned, they would not be among its people, while those who fear their Lord unseen will have forgiveness and a great reward. The surah points to the earth made easy to live on and the birds held up in the air only by the Most Merciful, and warns that Allah could make the earth swallow them. He gave people hearing, sight and hearts, yet few are grateful. It ends by asking who could bring them flowing water if their water sank into the earth. The Prophet ﷺ said that a surah of thirty ayahs interceded for a man until he was forgiven, and named this surah (Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, graded hasan), and he would not sleep until he had recited As-Sajdah and Al-Mulk (al-Tirmidhi, graded sahih by al-Albani).
The noble character of the Prophet ﷺ, and patience with the deniers.

Al-Qalam is an early Makkan surah, revealed when the Quraysh were calling the Prophet ﷺ insane and wanted him to compromise with them. Allah swears by the pen and what people write that the Prophet ﷺ is not mad, that he will have an unending reward, and that he is of great moral character; when asked about his character, Aishah said that his character was the Quran (Sahih Muslim). He is told not to obey the deniers, who wish he would soften so they could soften. The owners of a garden who planned to harvest it secretly and deprive the poor found it destroyed, an example of how wealth is a test. The righteous will have gardens of delight, and on the Day when people are called to prostrate, those who refused when they were able will be unable to. The Prophet ﷺ is told to be patient and not to be like the companion of the fish, Yunus, and the surah closes by saying the Quran is a reminder to all the worlds.
The Inevitable Reality of the Day of Judgment, and the truth of the Quran.

Al-Haqqah is a Makkan surah addressed to those who denied the resurrection and called the Prophet ﷺ a poet and a soothsayer. It opens with the Inevitable Reality, the Day of Judgment, and recalls how Thamud, 'Ad, Pharaoh and the overturned towns were destroyed, while those with Nuh were carried in the ship. It describes the single blast of the trumpet, the crushing of the earth and mountains, the splitting of the sky, and eight angels bearing the Throne, with nothing hidden. The one given his record in his right hand rejoices and enters a lofty garden, while the one given it in his left hand wishes he had never received it, for he did not believe in Allah the Most Great nor urge the feeding of the poor. Allah swears that the Quran is the word conveyed by a noble messenger, not the words of a poet or soothsayer, and that had the Prophet ﷺ invented anything, Allah would have seized him. It closes: the Quran is certain truth, so glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great.
Beautiful patience, and the qualities that save a person from the Fire.

Al-Ma'arij is a Makkan surah revealed when the disbelievers mockingly demanded the punishment they were warned of. It describes the punishment that will certainly come from Allah, Owner of the ways of ascent, to whom the angels and the Spirit ascend in a Day whose length is fifty thousand years, and tells the Prophet ﷺ to show beautiful patience. On that Day the sky will be like molten metal and the mountains like wool, no friend will ask about a friend, and the criminal will wish to ransom himself with his children, spouse, brother and everyone on earth. Man is created anxious, impatient in hardship and stingy in good times, except those who pray: they are constant in prayer, give a known share of their wealth to the one who asks and the deprived, believe in the Day of Judgment, fear their Lord's punishment, guard their chastity, keep their trusts and promises, uphold their testimony and guard their prayers; they will be honored in gardens. The disbelievers are left until the Day they come out of their graves with downcast eyes.
Nuh's patient call to his people over many years.

Nuh is a Makkan surah telling the story of Nuh's long call to his people, an example of patience in conveying the message. Nuh warns his people to worship Allah, fear Him and obey him, so that their sins are forgiven. He tells his Lord how he called them night and day, openly and privately, yet they put their fingers in their ears and grew more arrogant. He urged them to seek forgiveness, promising rain, wealth, children, gardens and rivers, and pointed to Allah's signs in their creation, the heavens, the moon, the sun and the earth. They disobeyed, followed leaders whose wealth only increased their loss, and clung to their idols Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr; Ibn Abbas explained that these were the names of righteous men whose statues were later worshipped once knowledge was forgotten (Sahih al-Bukhari). They were drowned, and Nuh prayed against the disbelievers and asked forgiveness for himself, his parents, and all believing men and women.
The jinn who heard the Quran and believed, and pure worship of Allah alone.

Al-Jinn is a Makkan surah. Ibn Abbas reported that a group of jinn heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting the Quran while leading his Companions in the Fajr prayer at Nakhlah, on the way to the market of 'Ukaz; they believed and went back to warn their people, and Allah revealed this surah (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). The jinn describe the wondrous Quran that guides to what is right, declare that their Lord has taken no wife or son, admit that the foolish among them spoke lies about Allah, and tell how the heaven is now guarded. Among the jinn are those who submit to Allah and those who deviate. The places of worship belong to Allah, so no one is to be called upon besides Him. The Prophet ﷺ is told to say that he calls only upon his Lord, has no power to harm or guide anyone, and can only convey the message. It ends: only Allah knows the unseen, and He reveals of it what He wills to a messenger He chooses.
Preparing the Prophet ﷺ through night prayer for the weight of revelation.

Al-Muzzammil is one of the earliest Makkan surahs. The Prophet ﷺ, wrapped in his garments, is told to stand in prayer at night and to recite the Quran slowly and clearly, for a weighty word will be sent down to him. Rising at night leaves a deeper impression and makes recitation more upright; he is to remember his Lord, devote himself to Him and take Him as his Guardian. He is told to be patient with what the deniers say and leave them to Allah, and the deniers are warned of a Day that will turn children grey, as Pharaoh was seized for disobeying the messenger sent to him. The last ayah lightens the night prayer, telling the believers to recite what is easy, since some are ill, traveling for provision or fighting in Allah's cause, and commands prayer, zakah and seeking Allah's forgiveness. Aishah reported that night prayer was made obligatory by the opening of this surah, and that after a year Allah revealed its ending, which made it voluntary (Sahih Muslim).
The command to arise and warn, and the fate of those who reject the Quran.

Al-Muddaththir is among the very first surahs revealed, at the start of the Prophet's ﷺ mission in Makkah. Jabir ibn Abdullah reported that after a pause in revelation, the Prophet ﷺ saw the angel who had come to him at Hira seated between the sky and the earth; frightened, he went home asking to be wrapped up, and Allah revealed its opening (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). He is commanded to arise and warn, magnify his Lord, purify his garments, shun idols and be patient for his Lord. Allah warns a man He blessed with wealth and sons who, after thinking and calculating, dismissed the Quran as magic; the commentators identify him as al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. Nineteen angels guard the Fire, a number that tests the disbelievers and increases the believers in faith. Every soul is held in pledge for its deeds; the criminals in the Fire say they did not pray, did not feed the poor, and denied the Day of Judgment. It ends: the Quran is a reminder for whoever wills, and Allah alone is worthy to be feared and to forgive.
The certainty of the resurrection, and the moment of death.

Al-Qiyamah is a Makkan surah answering those who denied that the dead would be raised. Allah swears by the Day of Resurrection and by the self-reproaching soul that He will gather man's bones, and is able to restore even his fingertips.
