Man wants to keep on sinning and mockingly asks when that Day will be; then sight will be dazzled, the moon eclipsed, and there will be no refuge except with Allah, and man will be a witness against himself despite his excuses. Ibn Abbas reported that the Prophet ﷺ used to move his tongue hurriedly to memorize the revelation, so Allah told him not to hasten, for its collection, recitation and explanation are upon Allah (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). On that Day some faces will be radiant, looking at their Lord, as authentic hadiths confirm, and others gloomy. The surah describes the moment of death when the soul reaches the collarbones, and ends: does man think he will be left without purpose, when Allah created him from a drop and is able to give life to the dead?
Man's creation and test, and the reward of those who feed others for Allah's sake.

Scholars differ on whether Al-Insan was revealed in Makkah or Madinah. Man passed a time when he was nothing worth mentioning; Allah created him from a mixed drop to test him, gave him hearing and sight, and showed him the way, whether he is grateful or ungrateful. Chains and a blazing Fire await the disbelievers. The righteous fulfil their vows, fear a Day of widespread evil, and feed the poor, the orphan and the captive, seeking only Allah's Face and wanting no reward or thanks. Allah protects them from that Day's evil and rewards them with a garden and silk, shade, low-hanging fruit, silver vessels, and a drink from the spring of Salsabil. The Quran was sent down in stages; the Prophet ﷺ is told to be patient, not to obey any sinner or disbeliever, and to remember his Lord morning, evening and at night. It ends: no one wills anything unless Allah wills, and He admits whom He wills into His mercy. The Prophet ﷺ used to recite As-Sajdah and Al-Insan in the Fajr prayer on Friday (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
Woe on that Day to the deniers.

Al-Mursalat is a Makkan surah stressing the certainty of the Day of Judgment to those who denied it. Ibn Mas'ud reported that it was revealed while the Companions were with the Prophet ﷺ in a cave at Mina, and they learned it from him fresh as it came down (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). Allah swears by those sent forth in succession, explained as the winds or the angels, that what you are promised will surely happen. On the Day of Sorting the stars will be blotted out, the sky opened and the mountains blown away, and the warning "Woe that Day to the deniers" is repeated ten times through the surah. Allah reminds them of earlier nations destroyed, of their creation from a lowly fluid, and of the earth that holds the living and the dead. The deniers will be driven to a shadow of smoke that gives no shade, while the righteous enjoy shade, springs and fruit. It ends: when told to bow in prayer, they do not, so in what message after this will they believe? Umm al-Fadl heard the Prophet ﷺ recite it in the Maghrib prayer, the last recitation she heard from him (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
The great news of the resurrection, and the Day of Sorting.

An-Naba is a Makkan surah answering those who disputed among themselves about the resurrection, which most commentators explain as "the great news" it mentions. Allah points to His creation: the earth as a resting place, mountains as pegs, people in pairs, sleep for rest, night as a covering, day for earning a living, seven strong heavens, a blazing lamp, and rain that brings grain, plants and gardens. The Day of Sorting is fixed: the trumpet is blown, people come in crowds, the sky opens and the mountains vanish like a mirage. Hell lies in wait for the transgressors as a fitting recompense, because they denied Allah's signs while every deed was recorded. The righteous will have gardens and a generous reward from their Lord. On that Day the Spirit and the angels will stand in rows, none speaking except whom the Most Merciful permits, and the disbeliever will say, "I wish I were dust."
The resurrection is certain, and the lesson of Pharaoh's arrogance.

An-Nazi'at is a Makkan surah answering those who denied the resurrection and mockingly asked when the Hour would come. Allah swears by the angels who draw out souls, harshly from some and gently from others, as most commentators explain. On the Day of the first and second blast, hearts will tremble; the deniers ask whether they will be restored after becoming decayed bones, yet it will take only a single cry. The story of Musa follows: called by his Lord in the sacred valley of Tuwa, he was sent to Pharaoh to invite him to purify himself; Pharaoh denied and proclaimed "I am your lord, the most high", so Allah seized him as a lesson for those who fear. Allah asks whether people are harder to create than the heaven He built. When the Great Overwhelming Event comes, whoever transgressed and preferred this world will have Hell as his refuge, and whoever feared standing before his Lord and restrained his desires will have Paradise. Knowledge of the Hour is with Allah alone; the Prophet ﷺ is only a warner.
Every sincere seeker of guidance deserves attention, whatever his status.

'Abasa is a Makkan surah. Aishah reported that it was revealed about Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, a blind man who came asking the Prophet ﷺ for guidance while the Prophet ﷺ was busy with one of the leaders of the idolaters, and turned away from him (Jami' al-Tirmidhi, graded sahih by al-Albani). Allah gently admonishes the Prophet ﷺ for frowning and turning from the blind man who came seeking to purify himself, while attending to one who considered himself in no need. The Quran is a reminder for whoever wills, written in honored pages by noble scribes. Man is ungrateful: Allah created him from a drop, eased his path, will cause him to die and will raise him, yet he has not done what he was commanded. Let him look at his food: rain, grain, fruit and pasture, provision for him and his livestock. When the Deafening Blast comes, a person will flee from his brother, mother, father, spouse and children, each concerned only with himself; some faces will be bright and joyful, and others covered in dust and darkness.
The overwhelming events of the Day of Judgment, and the Quran brought by Jibril.

At-Takwir is a Makkan surah describing the upheaval of the Day of Judgment to those who denied it. It lists the events of that Day: the sun wrapped up, the stars falling, the mountains moved, the seas set ablaze, souls paired, the baby girl buried alive asked for what sin she was killed, the records spread open, Hell set blazing and Paradise brought near; then every soul will know what it has brought. Allah swears that the Quran is the word conveyed by a noble messenger, Jibril, mighty and trusted. The Prophet ﷺ is not mad; he saw Jibril on the clear horizon, and the Quran is not the word of an accursed devil. It is a reminder to the worlds for whoever wills to go straight, though no one wills unless Allah wills. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever wishes to see the Day of Resurrection as if with his own eyes should read At-Takwir, Al-Infitar and Al-Inshiqaq (al-Tirmidhi, graded sahih by al-Albani).
What deceived man about his Generous Lord?

Al-Infitar is a Makkan surah reminding man of the Day of Recompense. When the sky splits, the stars scatter, the seas burst forth and the graves are overturned, every soul will know what it sent ahead and what it left behind. Allah asks man what deceived him about his Generous Lord, who created him, shaped him in proportion and formed him as He willed. Yet people deny the Recompense, while noble angels record all they do. The righteous will be in bliss and the wicked in the Fire, which they cannot escape. On that Day no soul will be able to help another, and the command belongs wholly to Allah. It is one of the three surahs the Prophet ﷺ named for whoever wishes to see the Day of Resurrection as if with his own eyes (al-Tirmidhi, graded sahih by al-Albani).
Honesty in dealings, and the records of the wicked and the righteous.

Scholars differ on whether Al-Mutaffifin was revealed in Makkah or Madinah. Ibn Abbas reported that when the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah, its people were among the worst in giving short measure, so Allah revealed this surah, and they improved their measures afterwards (Ibn Majah and al-Nasa'i, graded hasan). It warns those who take full measure from others but give less when they measure or weigh for them: do they not think they will be raised for a great Day before the Lord of the worlds? The record of the wicked is in Sijjin; their sins have covered their hearts like rust, so they will be screened from their Lord. The Prophet ﷺ explained that each sin leaves a black spot on the heart that spreads unless the person repents, and that this is the rust mentioned in this surah (al-Tirmidhi, graded hasan sahih). The record of the righteous is in 'Illiyyin; they will be on couches with faces glowing with bliss, given a sealed drink whose seal is musk, so let those who compete, compete for this. The disbelievers used to laugh at the believers, but on that Day the believers will laugh at them.
Man's journey to meet his Lord, and the reckoning.

Al-Inshiqaq is a Makkan surah about the Day of Judgment and the reckoning. When the sky splits open and the earth casts out what is in it, both obeying their Lord, man, toiling steadily towards his Lord, will meet Him. Whoever is given his record in his right hand will have an easy reckoning and return to his people joyful; the Prophet ﷺ explained that this easy reckoning is only the presentation of deeds, while whoever is questioned in detail will be punished (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim, from Aishah). Whoever is given his record behind his back will cry out for destruction; he was happy among his people and thought he would never return to Allah. Allah swears by the twilight, the night and the moon that people will pass from stage to stage. It asks why they do not believe and do not prostrate when the Quran is recited to them; Abu Hurayrah prostrated in this surah and said he had seen the Prophet ﷺ do so (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). It is also one of the three surahs named for whoever wishes to see the Day of Resurrection as if with his own eyes.
Comfort for persecuted believers: Allah witnesses everything.

Al-Buruj is a Makkan surah revealed while the believers were being persecuted for their faith, reminding them that earlier believers endured the same and that Allah witnesses everything. Allah swears by the sky with its great stars and the promised Day. Cursed were the people of the ditch, who burned believers in a pit of fire while watching, resenting them only because they believed in Allah, the Mighty, the Praiseworthy. Many commentators, including Ibn Kathir, explain this with the story of the boy, the king and the monk reported in Sahih Muslim. Those who persecute believing men and women and do not repent face the punishment of Hell, while the believers who do righteous deeds will have gardens, the great success. Allah's grip is severe; He is the Forgiving, the Loving, Owner of the Glorious Throne, who does whatever He wills. The fate of Pharaoh and Thamud is recalled, and it ends: this is a glorious Quran in a Preserved Tablet.
Over every soul there is a guardian, and Allah can bring man back to life.

At-Tariq is a Makkan surah affirming that Allah, who created man, is able to bring him back to life. Allah swears by the sky and the night-comer, the piercing star, that over every soul there is a guardian. Let man consider what he was created from, a gushing fluid; the One who created him is able to bring him back, on the Day when secrets are laid bare and he has no strength or helper. Allah swears by the sky that returns rain and the earth that splits with plants that the Quran is a decisive word, not a jest. The disbelievers are plotting, and Allah too is planning, so give them respite for a while.
Glorifying Allah the Most High; the Hereafter is better and more lasting.

Al-A'la is a Makkan surah. The Prophet ﷺ is told to glorify the name of his Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, decreed and guided, and brought out pasture and then turned it into dark stubble. Allah promises that he will recite the Quran and not forget, except what Allah wills, and that He will ease his way to ease. He is to remind wherever reminding benefits: whoever fears Allah will take heed, while the most wretched will avoid it and enter the great Fire. Successful is the one who purifies himself, remembers his Lord's name and prays, yet people prefer this world, though the Hereafter is better and more lasting; this is in the earlier scriptures of Ibrahim and Musa. The Prophet ﷺ used to recite Al-A'la and Al-Ghashiyah in the Eid and Friday prayers (Sahih Muslim).
The Overwhelming Event, and reflecting on Allah's creation.

Al-Ghashiyah is a Makkan surah about the Overwhelming Event, the Day of Judgment. On that Day some faces will be humbled and exhausted, entering a scorching Fire, with drink from a boiling spring and food that neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger. Other faces will be joyful, pleased with their efforts, in a lofty garden with no idle talk, flowing springs and raised couches. It asks: do they not look at the camels, how they were created; the sky, how it was raised; the mountains, how they were set firm; and the earth, how it was spread out? The Prophet ﷺ is only to remind; he is not a controller over them. Whoever turns away and disbelieves, Allah will punish; to Him is their return and their reckoning. The Prophet ﷺ used to recite it with Al-A'la in the Eid and Friday prayers (Sahih Muslim).
Wealth and poverty are both a test, and the call to the soul at peace.

Al-Fajr is a Makkan surah. Allah swears by the dawn and the ten nights, which most commentators, such as Ibn Kathir, explain as the first ten nights of Dhul-Hijjah. He recalls how He dealt with 'Ad of Iram with its lofty pillars, Thamud who carved the rocks in the valley, and Pharaoh, who all spread corruption until their Lord poured punishment on them. When man is given plenty he says his Lord has honored him, and when his provision is restricted he says his Lord has humiliated him; yet people do not honor the orphan, do not urge feeding the poor, consume inheritance greedily and love wealth excessively. When the earth is crushed and Hell is brought near, man will remember and wish he had sent ahead good for his life. The Prophet ﷺ said that Hell will be brought that Day with seventy thousand reins, each held by seventy thousand angels (Sahih Muslim). The surah ends with the call to the soul at peace: return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing to Him, and enter My Paradise.
Man is created in toil, and the steep path of good deeds.

Al-Balad is a Makkan surah. Allah swears by the city of Makkah, and by a father and his offspring, that man is created in toil and hardship. Man thinks no one has power over him and boasts of the wealth he has spent, as if no one sees him, yet Allah gave him two eyes, a tongue and lips, and showed him the two ways of good and evil. He has not attempted the steep path: freeing a slave, or feeding on a day of hunger an orphaned relative or a poor person in misery, and then being among those who believe and urge one another to patience and to mercy; they are the companions of the right. Those who deny Allah's signs are the companions of the left, with a Fire closed over them.
Purifying the soul is success, and corrupting it is failure.

Ash-Shams is a Makkan surah. Allah swears by the sun and its brightness, the moon, the day and the night, the sky and the earth, and by the soul and how He proportioned it and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness: successful is the one who purifies it, and failed is the one who corrupts it. As an example, Thamud denied their messenger Salih out of transgression; though he warned them about the she-camel of Allah and her turn to drink, they denied him and hamstrung her, so their Lord destroyed them. The Prophet ﷺ used to pray: "O Allah, grant my soul its taqwa and purify it, for You are the best to purify it" (Sahih Muslim).
People's efforts differ: giving leads to ease, and stinginess to hardship.

Al-Layl is a Makkan surah. Allah swears by the night, the day and the creation of male and female that people's efforts are diverse. Whoever gives, fears Allah and affirms the best, Allah will ease his way to ease; whoever is stingy, thinks himself free of need and denies the best, Allah will ease his way to hardship, and his wealth will not help him when he falls. Guidance is from Allah, and to Him belong the Hereafter and this world. The blazing Fire is for the most wretched, who denied and turned away, while the most righteous will be kept far from it: the one who gives his wealth to purify himself, seeking only the Face of his Lord, the Most High, and he will be well pleased. Ali reported that the Prophet ﷺ said everyone's place has been written, and when asked whether they should rely on that, he said, "Work, for each person is eased towards what he was created for", and recited this surah's ayahs on giving and ease (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
Allah has not abandoned His Prophet ﷺ: comfort and gratitude.

Ad-Duha is an early Makkan surah of comfort for the Prophet ﷺ. Jundub ibn Abdullah reported that when revelation paused for a short time, the idolaters taunted that his Lord had abandoned him, and Allah revealed this surah (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). Allah swears by the morning brightness and the still night that He has neither abandoned the Prophet ﷺ nor hated him, that the Hereafter is better for him than this life, and that his Lord will give him until he is satisfied. He reminds him that He found him an orphan and sheltered him, found him without knowledge of the revelation and guided him, and found him in need and made him self-sufficient. So he is not to oppress the orphan, nor turn away the one who asks, and he is to speak of the blessings of his Lord.
With hardship comes ease.

Ash-Sharh is an early Makkan surah of comfort for the Prophet ﷺ, close in theme to Ad-Duha. Allah reminds the Prophet ﷺ that He expanded his chest, removed the burden that weighed down his back, and raised his mention; commentators explain the last as his name being mentioned with Allah's, as in the testimony of faith and the call to prayer. Twice it affirms that with hardship comes ease. When he is free from his tasks, he is to strive in worship and turn to his Lord with longing.
Man was created in the best form, and faith keeps him from falling low.

At-Tin is a Makkan surah. Allah swears by the fig and the olive, by Mount Sinai, and by this secure city of Makkah that He created man in the best form, then returned him to the lowest of the low, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, who will have an unending reward. So what makes anyone deny the Recompense after this? Is Allah not the most just of judges? Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib heard the Prophet ﷺ recite this surah in the Isha prayer on a journey, and said he had never heard anyone with a better voice or recitation (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
The first revelation: read in the name of your Lord.

The first five ayahs of Al-'Alaq were the first revelation of the Quran, received by the Prophet ﷺ in the cave of Hira, as Aishah reported (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). The Prophet ﷺ is commanded to read in the name of his Lord, who created man from a clinging clot, and who in His generosity taught by the pen and taught man what he did not know. Man transgresses when he sees himself as self-sufficient, though all will return to Allah. The rest of the surah concerns Abu Jahl, who threatened to step on the Prophet's ﷺ neck if he saw him praying at the Ka'bah (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). Allah condemns the one who stops a servant of His from praying, reminds him that Allah sees, and warns that he will be seized by the forelock. It ends: do not obey him, but prostrate and draw near to Allah.
The Night of Decree, better than a thousand months.

Scholars differ on whether Al-Qadr was revealed in Makkah or Madinah. Allah sent down the Quran on the Night of Decree, which is in Ramadan. That night is better than a thousand months; the angels and the Spirit, Jibril, descend in it by their Lord's permission with every matter, and it is peace until the break of dawn. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever stands in prayer on Laylat al-Qadr out of faith and hoping for reward will have his past sins forgiven (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim), and told the believers to seek it in the odd nights of the last ten nights of Ramadan (Sahih al-Bukhari).
The clear evidence, and sincere worship as the upright religion.

Scholars differ on whether Al-Bayyinah was revealed in Makkah or Madinah. The disbelievers among the People of the Book and the idolaters were not going to leave their ways until clear evidence came to them: a Messenger from Allah reciting purified pages. The People of the Book divided only after this evidence came, though they were commanded only to worship Allah sincerely, establish prayer and give zakah; that is the upright religion. Those who disbelieve are the worst of creatures, while those who believe and do righteous deeds are the best of creatures; their reward is the Gardens of Eden, and Allah is pleased with them and they with Him. The Prophet ﷺ told Ubayy ibn Ka'b that Allah had commanded him to recite this surah to him; Ubayy asked whether Allah had named him, and when told yes, he wept (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
Every deed, even an atom's weight, will be seen.

Scholars differ on whether Az-Zalzalah was revealed in Makkah or Madinah. It describes the final earthquake, when the earth throws out its burdens and, by its Lord's command, reports everything that was done upon it. On that Day people will come forth in scattered groups to be shown their deeds, and nothing will be lost: every good deed and every evil deed, even the weight of an atom, will be seen. The Prophet ﷺ described its closing ayahs as unique and all-encompassing (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
Man's ingratitude and love of wealth.

Scholars differ on whether Al-'Adiyat was revealed in Makkah or Madinah. Allah swears by the charging horses, panting, striking sparks with their hooves and raiding at dawn, that man is ungrateful to his Lord, is himself a witness to that, and is intense in his love of wealth. It reminds him that when the graves are emptied and what is hidden in the hearts is brought out, his Lord will be fully aware of everything he did.
The Striking Calamity, and the weighing of deeds.

Al-Qari'ah is a Makkan surah about the Day of Judgment, which it calls the Striking Calamity. It describes the terror of that Day, when people will be scattered like moths and the mighty mountains will be like fluffed wool. Then deeds will be weighed: the one whose good deeds are heavy will have a pleasing life, while the one whose good deeds are light will have Hawiyah, a blazing Fire, as his refuge.
Competing for more of this world distracts people until the grave.

At-Takathur is a Makkan surah. It warns that competing for more and more of this world distracts people from what matters until they reach their graves. They will surely come to know the truth; they will see the Fire with their own eyes, and on that Day they will be asked about every blessing they enjoyed. While reciting this surah, the Prophet ﷺ said that the son of Adam says "My wealth, my wealth", yet he has of it only what he ate and used up, wore and wore out, or gave in charity and sent ahead (Sahih Muslim).
The way out of loss: faith, good deeds, truth and patience.

Al-'Asr is a Makkan surah. Allah swears by time that all mankind is in loss, except those who have four qualities: they believe, they do righteous deeds, and they urge one another to the truth and to patience. Ibn Kathir reports that Imam al-Shafi'i said that if people reflected on this surah alone, it would be enough for them.
A warning to the slanderer who hoards wealth.

Al-Humazah is a Makkan surah. It warns the person who slanders and finds fault with others, and who gathers wealth and keeps counting it, thinking it will make him last forever. Such a person will be thrown into al-Hutamah, the Crusher: the kindled Fire of Allah that reaches up to the hearts and is closed in over them.
Allah's protection of the Ka'bah in the Year of the Elephant.

Al-Fil is a Makkan surah recalling the Year of the Elephant, when Abrahah's army from Yemen marched with an elephant to destroy the Ka'bah; according to the sirah, the Prophet ﷺ was born in that year. Allah reminds the Quraysh how He made the plot of the people of the elephant fail, sending against them birds in flocks that struck them with stones of baked clay, leaving them like eaten-up straw. At al-Hudaybiyah, when the Prophet's ﷺ camel knelt and would not move, he said she had been held back by the One who held back the elephant (Sahih al-Bukhari).
The Quraysh should thank Allah for their security and provision.

Quraysh is a Makkan surah closely linked in meaning to Al-Fil, as many commentators note. It reminds the Quraysh of Allah's favor in making their winter and summer journeys safe and familiar, which commentators explain as their trading caravans to Yemen in winter and to Syria in summer. So they should worship the Lord of this House, who fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear.
True faith shows in caring for others and in sincere prayer.

Al-Ma'un is listed as Makkan, though some scholars held that part or all of it was revealed in Madinah. It describes the one who denies the Day of Recompense: he harshly drives away the orphan and does not urge others to feed the poor. It then warns those who pray but are heedless of their prayer, who do their deeds only to be seen, and who refuse even small acts of help (al-ma'un).
Allah's abundant gift to the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-Kawthar is the shortest surah of the Quran, and scholars differ on whether it was revealed in Makkah or Madinah. It tells the Prophet ﷺ that Allah has given him al-Kawthar, so he should pray to his Lord and sacrifice for Him alone, and that it is his enemy, not he, who is cut off from all good. Anas reported that the Prophet ﷺ, after a light sleep, raised his head smiling, recited this surah as just revealed, and explained that al-Kawthar is a river in Paradise his Lord promised him, with a pool to which his nation will come on the Day of Resurrection (Sahih Muslim). Ibn Abbas explained al-Kawthar as the abundant good Allah gave him, which includes that river (Sahih al-Bukhari).
Complete separation between worshipping Allah alone and idol worship.

Al-Kafirun is a Makkan surah declaring complete separation between the worship of Allah alone and the worship of idols. The Prophet ﷺ is told to declare clearly to the disbelievers that he will never worship what they worship and they do not worship what he worships, so there can be no mixing of the two: they have their religion and he has his. The Prophet ﷺ used to recite it with Al-Ikhlas in the two sunnah rak'ahs before Fajr (Sahih Muslim).
Allah's help and victory, and turning to Him in praise and repentance.

An-Nasr is a Madinan surah, among the very last revealed; Ibn Abbas said it was the last complete surah to be revealed (Sahih Muslim). It tells the Prophet ﷺ that when Allah's help and the victory come, which most commentators explain as the conquest of Makkah, and people enter Allah's religion in crowds, he should glorify his Lord with praise and seek His forgiveness, for He always accepts repentance. Ibn Abbas understood it as a sign that the Prophet's ﷺ life was nearing its end, and Umar agreed (Sahih al-Bukhari). Aishah reported that after it was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ often said in his bowing and prostration: "Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You; O Allah, forgive me" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
The fate of Abu Lahab, who opposed the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-Masad is an early Makkan surah, revealed after the Prophet ﷺ began calling his people openly. Ibn Abbas reported that when the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to warn his closest relatives, he climbed al-Safa and called the clans of Quraysh, warning them of a severe punishment; his uncle Abu Lahab said, "May you perish! Is it for this you gathered us?", and Allah revealed this surah (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). It declares that Abu Lahab will perish, that his wealth and gains will not help him, and that he will burn in a blazing Fire, along with his wife, who joined him in harming the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Lahab and his wife lived for years after it was revealed and died as disbelievers, as the surah foretold.
The pure Oneness of Allah (tawhid).

Scholars differ on whether Al-Ikhlas was revealed in Makkah or Madinah. It is a pure statement of tawhid: it teaches that Allah is One and unique, that all creation depends on Him while He depends on no one, that He has no child and no parent, and that nothing is equal or comparable to Him. The Prophet ﷺ said it is equal to a third of the Quran (Sahih al-Bukhari). When a Companion who led prayers always ended his recitation with it because it describes the Most Merciful, the Prophet ﷺ said, "Tell him that Allah loves him" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). Each night before sleeping, the Prophet ﷺ recited it with Al-Falaq and An-Nas, blew into his palms and wiped over his body (Sahih al-Bukhari).
Seeking refuge in Allah from all harm in His creation.

Scholars differ on whether Al-Falaq was revealed in Makkah or Madinah. With An-Nas it forms the two surahs of seeking refuge (al-Mu'awwidhatayn). It teaches the believer to seek protection with Allah, the Lord of daybreak, from every harm in His creation, from the dangers of the darkness of night, from sorcery, and from the harm of the envier when he envies. Uqbah ibn Amir reported that the Prophet ﷺ said ayahs had been revealed that night the like of which had never been seen: Al-Falaq and An-Nas (Sahih Muslim). The Prophet ﷺ recited them before sleeping, and over himself when ill (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
Seeking refuge in Allah from the hidden whispers of Shaytan.

An-Nas is the last surah of the Quran, and scholars differ on whether it was revealed in Makkah or Madinah. It teaches the believer to seek protection with Allah, the Lord, King and God of mankind, from an enemy he cannot see: "the whisperer who withdraws". This is Shaytan, who puts doubts, bad thoughts and temptations to sin into people's hearts, and who pulls back when a person remembers Allah. These whisperers can be jinn, or humans who call others to evil. The protection is remembering Allah and turning to Him. With Al-Falaq it forms the two surahs of seeking refuge, which the Prophet ﷺ recited before sleep and when ill, and taught to be recited after every prayer (Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i, graded sahih by al-Albani).
